analysis.one_liner: Bans meatpackers' opaque livestock forward contracts that lack firm, publicly bid prices.
analysis.headline: The bill, which drew bipartisan sponsorship from four senators, died in the Senate Agriculture Committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Big meatpackers often buy cattle and hogs months ahead using secret formula prices instead of open bidding, so ranchers and farmers may not learn what their animals are really worth until after the deal is done. This bill would have required forward contracts to carry a firm dollar price set on the day of signing, be offered through open, public bidding, and banned formula pricing and very large off-market sales, with exceptions for farmer-owned cooperatives and small packers. The bill was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Independent cattle ranchers and hog farmers, who would sell into open markets with visible prices instead of accepting packers' formula offers, and potentially consumers, if more transparent livestock prices make the beef and pork markets more competitive.

how_it_helps.text: Forward contracts could no longer be signed without a firm base price that equals a fixed dollar amount on the day the contract is signed, so sellers would know what they were being paid before committing.
Contracts would have to be offered for bid in an open, public manner where buyers and sellers can participate in and witness the bids, replacing privately negotiated deals with visible competition.
Formula prices — deals pegged to a price not determined until after the contract is signed — would be banned, as would forward sales of more than 40 cattle or 30 hogs outside the open-bidding rules.
Exceptions would preserve marketing channels for farmer-owned cooperatives and packers with a single processing plant, targeting the rules at the largest packers.

analysis.who_pays: Large meatpacking companies, which would lose the ability to buy livestock at private, formula-based prices negotiated outside public markets, and some large-scale producers who currently lock in big volumes through such contracts.

drawbacks.text: Limiting forward sales to 40 cattle or 30 hogs without open bidding could make it harder for very large feeding operations to move livestock in bulk, which the bill itself acknowledges by allowing the Agriculture Secretary to adjust the quantity caps for advances in marketing and transportation.

Formula pricing and private contracts can hedge price risk for both sides of large transactions; the bill's definition carefully excludes futures-market pricing from the formula-price ban, but critics of such restrictions have argued they reduce marketing flexibility and could push sales through fewer channels.
The cooperative and single-plant packer exemptions mean the rules fall unevenly across the industry, leaving some buyers free to use the contracts the largest packers could not.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For independent ranchers and hog farmers, the price transparency rules address a real problem: contracts signed before anyone knows the price. The quantity caps and drafting are blunt instruments, and the exemptions carve out some of the very players the open-market principle is meant to cover, but the core requirement — a firm, publicly bid price — is straightforward and targeted at concentrated buyers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 20, 2009 by Sen. Enzi together with Sens. Dorgan, Johnson, and Grassley, a group spanning both parties.
On the same day it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry.
The action history shows no further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor consideration — before the 111th Congress ended in early January 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large meatpacking companies, which kept the ability to buy cattle and hogs on private, formula-priced contracts, while livestock producers got no relief.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by two Republicans (Enzi of Wyoming, Grassley of Iowa) and two Democrats (Dorgan of North Dakota, Johnson of South Dakota) with additional cosponsors from both parties; it never advanced far enough for a party-line vote.

industries.note: The bill would have banned the formula-priced and privately bid forward contracts the largest packers use to buy livestock outside public markets, forcing them to bid visibly against other buyers. Transparent bidding can raise what ranchers are paid, which comes out of packers' margins.

The bill explicitly exempted cooperatives majority-owned by members who supply livestock, packers too small to report daily purchases, and packers with one plant — giving them a carve-out while larger competitors face the new rules.

industries.industry: Independent cattle ranchers and hog producers
industries.note: Producers would sell under firm, openly bid prices instead of accepting formula prices set after the fact, giving them clearer information and more bargaining power against concentrated buyers.
